name: SIRTOM — Shared composters launch campaign
description: Communication campaign for the launch of shared composters across a public waste authority's territory, produced by an agency. I took part in the brief and the decisions; my proposal to lead with the financial impact was not kept, but the final campaign builds on a close idea: the value we throw away.
context: Since 1 January 2024, French law (the AGEC anti-waste law) requires bio-waste from households to be sorted at source, and it is up to local authorities to provide the solution. If residents do not sort, the authority bears the consequences and the cost. To help residents do it, SIRTOM de la région Flers-Condé launched shared composters across its territory, in Normandy, and needed a campaign to announce them.

The campaign was designed and produced by an external agency, not by me. During my internship I took part in the decisions on what to brief the agency on, how to answer its proposals and what to ask for.

work.title: My proposal: talk money, not ecology
work.text: I suggested leading with the financial side: the real savings composting brings to the authority, which directly limits increases in the waste collection tax paid by residents.
points: My reading of the audience: the area was not very receptive to environmental messages, and a genuine ecology awareness campaign would need far more time and budget.
So the message had to speak to residents' immediate, practical concerns.

work.title: What was decided: the value we throw away
work.text: The direct financial argument was not kept. The final campaign stays on the same ground, though: food scraps as something valuable that gets wasted, rather than an environmental duty.
points: The tagline: “Your food scraps have real value. Don’t waste it: compost.”

The headline plays on French slang for money: “blé, oseille, radis, avoine, patates” are crops, and most of them also mean cash. Variants follow the same idea: “Balance le blé !”, “Par ici l’oseille !”, “Donne-moi des patates !”.
The brochure backs it with figures: food and green waste make up more than 30% of household bins, about 4,000 tonnes a year on the territory, and collecting and treating them costs more every year.

work.title: A compost wheel for children
work.text: A rotating cardboard disc shows, item by item, what can go in the composter, in moderation or not at all. The aim was assumed: make it playful enough to intrigue children.
points: Short term: children push their household to start composting.
Long term: they learn the habit very young, a slow but lasting investment in awareness.

work.title: Working with the agency
work.text: I took part in the back-and-forth with the agency: reviewing its proposals, deciding on the answers and on the requests to send back.

work.title: Where the campaign ran
work.text: One visual line, declined across every touchpoint.
points: Posters (main visual and three variants) and wind flags for events.
A composter-shaped flyer with a QR code to the authority's website.
A brochure explaining why and how to compost.
Tote bags, the compost wheel, SIRTOM's social media and the livery of the waste collection trucks.
